serverMetadata.instructions:
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions.

Here is the raw content: Contents of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NREL/resstock/develop/README.md: The `develop` branch is under active development. Find the latest release [here](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/releases). [![GitHub release (latest by date including pre-releases)](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/NREL/resstock?include_prereleases)](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/releases) [![ci](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/actions/workflows/config.yml/badge.svg?branch=develop)](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/actions/workflows/config.yml) [![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/resstock/badge/?version=latest)](https://resstock.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest) [ResStock™](https://www.nrel.gov/buildings/resstock.html), built on the [OpenStudio platform](http://openstudio.net), is a project geared at modeling existing residential building stocks at national, regional, or local scales with a high-degree of granularity (e.g., one physics-based simulation model for every 200 dwelling units), using the [EnergyPlus simulation engine](http://energyplus.net). Information about ComStock™, a sister tool for modeling the commercial building stock, can be found [here](https://www.nrel.gov/buildings/comstock.html). This repository contains: - [Housing characteristics of the U.S. residential building stock](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/tree/main/project_national/housing_characteristics), in the form of conditional probability distributions stored as tab-separated value (.tsv) files. Comments at the bottom of each file document data sources and assumptions for each. - [A library of housing characteristic "options"](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/blob/main/resources/options_lookup.tsv) that translate high-level characteristic parameters into arguments for OpenStudio measures, and which are referenced by the housing characteristic .tsv files and building energy upgrades defined in project definition files - Project definition [buildstockbatch YML files](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/blob/main/project_national/national_baseline.yml) openable in any text editor for v2.3.0 and later - Unit-level [OpenStudio-HPXML Measures](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/tree/main/resources/hpxml-measures) (v3.0.0 and later) for automatically constructing individual representative dwelling unit OpenStudio Models using [OpenStudio-HPXML](https://openstudio-hpxml.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest) - [Higher-level OpenStudio Measures](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/tree/main/measures) for controlling simulation inputs and outputs Software for running ResStock simulations: - [Versions 2.3.0](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/releases/tag/v2.3.0) and later only support the use of [buildstockbatch](https://github.com/NREL/buildstockbatch) for deploying simulations on high-performance or cloud computing. Version 2.3.0 also removed separate projects for single-family detached and multifamily buildings, in lieu of a combined `project_national` representing the U.S. residential building stock. See the [changelogs](https://resstock.readthedocs.io/en/latest/changelog/index.html) for more details. - For large-scale production runs of ResStock, it is recommended that [buildstockbatch](https://github.com/NREL/buildstockbatch) is used. For smaller-scale tests, [run_analysis.rb](https://github.com/NREL/resstock/blob/develop/workflow/run_analysis.rb) can be used. Information about the workflow can be found in ResStock's [documentation](https://resstock.readthedocs.io/en/latest/basic_tutorial/running_a_project.html#using-run-analysis-rb).

They vary by **when the thermostat changes, the temperature offset, and the duration**. [Release upgrade list](https://resstock.nlr.gov/datasets)\n\n| Upgrade | Strategy | Thermostat adjustment |\n|---|---|---|\n| **24** | On-peak load shedding, **2°F** | During the 4-hour peak window, lower the heating setpoint or raise the cooling setpoint by 2°F. |\n| **25** | **4-hour** pre-peak load shifting, **2°F** | For 4 hours before the peak window, preheat by raising the heating setpoint or precool by lowering the cooling setpoint by 2°F. |\n| **26** | On-peak load shedding, **4°F** | Same timing as 24, with a larger 4°F adjustment. |\n| **27** | **4-hour** pre-peak load shifting, **4°F** | Same timing as 25, with a larger 4°F adjustment. |\n| **28** | **1-hour** pre-peak load shifting, **2°F** | Same adjustment as 25, applied for only 1 hour before the peak window. |\n\nThese settings are documented in Table 8 of the [HVAC Load Flexibility report](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf#page=33).\n\n**Shedding** reduces conditioning during peak hours by allowing indoor temperatures to drift. **Shifting** conditions the building beforehand, using its thermal mass to reduce subsequent demand; the thermostat returns to its normal schedule during the peak window. The released measures do **not** combine preconditioning with an on-peak setback. Larger offsets and longer preconditioning generally provide greater flexibility. [Measure methodology](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf)\n\nOne modeling caveat: these scenarios dispatch flexibility nearly every day to characterize technical potential. Their annual savings should therefore not be interpreted directly as savings from a typical program with occasional events. [Dispatch limitations](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf#page=37)"}} ### -- Thermostat Demand Flexibility -- ###
  - upgrade_name: HVAC Demand Flexibility - On-peak Load Shedding, 2F Offset
    package_apply_logic: *has_cooling_or_heating

The HVAC demand flexibility measures are **upgrades 24–28**, corresponding to measure IDs **dr_001–dr_005**. They differ in whether they shed load during peak hours or shift it earlier, the thermostat offset, and the preconditioning duration. [ResStock release package list](https://resstock.nlr.gov/datasets)

|---|---|---|---|
| **24** | dr_001 | On-peak load shedding, **2°F** | Lower heating / raise cooling setpoints by 2°F during the peak period. |
| **25** | dr_002 | **4-hour** pre-peak load shifting, **2°F** | Preheat / precool by 2°F for four hours before the peak. |

| AC   | air conditioner                            |

## Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit end-use load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end -use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Heating, Ventilation, and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) Load Flexibility.

The HVAC load flexibility measure modifies the heating and cooling thermostat set points before peak periods to preheat or precool the building or during peak periods to shift load away from peak periods. In real deployments of demand flexibility via smart thermostats, the dispatch is typically limited to a handful of days per year to avoid customer fatigue. But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched nearly every day in the modeled dataset . Although the profile on any given day is realistic, the full annual load profiles do not reflect the realistic dispatch of HVAC load flexibility . Details on the appropriate use of the load profiles can be found in this document.

To keep the logic simple and to generate the most comprehensive result that can support different future analysis, this measure applies to all dwelling units with either a heating or a cooling system (approximately 99.7% of the dwelling units modeled in ResStock); however, the heating load analysis in this document is done on only buildings with electric heating. With a 4°F offset during the 4-hour peak periods across all 51 states, this resulted in an average reduction of 57% in peak period heating electricity consumption during the winter months and a 54% reduction in peak period cooling electricity during the summer months.

## Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit end-use load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end -use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock ™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Heating, Ventilation, and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) Load Flexibility.

The HVAC load flexibility measure modifies the heating and cooling thermostat set points before peak periods to preheat or precool the building or during peak periods to shift load away from peak periods. In real deployments of demand flexibility via smart thermostats, the dispatch is typically limited to a handful of days per year to avoid customer fatigue. But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched nearly every day in the modeled dataset . Although the profile on any given day is realistic, the full annual load profiles do not reflect the realistic dispatch of HVAC load flexibility . Details on the appropriate use of the load profiles can be found in this document.

To keep the logic simple and to generate the most comprehensive result that can support different future analysis, this measure applies to all dwelling units with either a heating or a cooling system (approximately 99.7% of the dwelling units modeled in ResStock); however, the heating load analysis in this document is done on only buildings with electric heating. With a 4°F offset during the 4-hour peak periods across all 51 states, this resulted in an average reduction of 57% in peak period heating electricity consumption during the winter months and a 54% reduction in peak period cooling electricity during the summer months.

## 1.2.5 Dispatch Strategy

In historic deployments, thermostat-based demand response is typically only dispatched 15 -25 days per year to avoid customer fatigue (Xcel, 2021) (Austin Energy, 2024). But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched every day in the modeled dataset . The dispatch strategy is modified for shoulder-season days where heating or cooling load is assumed to be minimal, defined by an average daily temperature greater than 50°F and less than 68°F. On those days, load shifting (done via precooling or preheating) is not dispatched, but load-shedding events are dispatched. The method for choosing this temperature range is described in section 4.2 Initial Sensitivity Analysis. Because of the unrealistically high number of days that demand flexibility is dispatched in this upgrade, the results must be used thoughtfully. One approach is to use daily profiles from the baseline for most days of the year and to splice in daily profiles from the upgrade for days when the intent of the analysis is to dispatch demand flexibility. Similarly, annualized energy consumption or energy savings metrics should not be used because of the overrepresentation of dispatch .

## 2 ResStock Baseline Approach

The baseline assumption for thermostats in ResStock is a range of heating and cooling set points and setbacks or setups derived from the Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020, which vary based on climate zone, building type, HVAC type, and tenure (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2023). These set points are assumed to apply year-round. Approximately one-third of dwelling units are assumed to have heating and/or cooling thermostat setbacks or setups, where the set point is changed by the homeowner during part of each day. The distribution of set points in the building stock is shown in Figure 1. ResStock makes no explicit assumption about whether these setbacks or setups are achieved using manual adjustment, a programmable thermostat, or a smart thermostat. In practice, demand response programs typically incentivize or directly pay for customers to install smart thermostats as a condition of program participation.

Figure 1. Distributions of thermostat set points, setups, and setbacks 1

Figure 1: four bar charts of dwelling units. Top: cooling setpoint and heating setpoint distributions by temperature bin; the commonest cooling bins hold 19% to 20% of dwellings each, the commonest heating bins 21% and 23%. Bottom: cooling set up, where 66% of dwellings use 0°F, 20% use 2°F, 9% use 5°F and 5% use 9°F; and heating set back, 58% at 0°F, 26% at 3°F, 12% at 6°F and 5% at 12°F.

## 3 Modeling Approach

## 3.1 Applicability

The goal of demand flexibility is to change the electric or gas load profile of the building in a meaningful way; therefore, this measure is applicable to all dwelling units with either a cooling system or a heating system. Although the measure shifts the load profile of the dwelling units with nonelectric heating during heating season, the change to the electric load profile is minimal because it only changes the fan or pump electricity consumption. For this reason, the heating load analysis in this document is focused on buildings with electric heating only. Table 4 summarizes the breakout of the building stock to which the measure applies and what is included in heating and cooling load analysis.

## 3.2  ResStock Workflow

Figure 2 illustrates the modeling approach used to integrate a load flexibility measure into ResStock. This measure modifies the existing building energy model thermostat set point schedules during the pre-peak and on-peak periods only. For times outside of the event, the existing thermostat schedules in the model are unchanged. If the baseline thermostat set point schedules indicate that the dwelling unit is already in a setback or a setup state, the demand flexibility thermostat change still applies.

The load flexibility scenario (which includes the pre-peak duration and the set point offset values) serves as input for the measure, allowing customized controls. The input values used for this measure are explained in section 3.3 Input Variables.

Figure 2. Modeling approach for running a load flexibility measure in ResStock

<!-- figure described by overlay: resstock_resstock_amy2018_2025_release_1/upgrade_measures/measure_pdfs/93846.yaml
     source: 93846_images/image_000003_06ad1ce32d34b0a4c47437dc4560d542e3896ac29aeb4ea0e7a85f2e95bb78c7.png

![Block diagram of the modeling approach: on-peak hour input, load flexibility measure, and results](93846_images/image_000003_06ad1ce32d34b0a4c47437dc4560d542e3896ac29aeb4ea0e7a85f2e95bb78c7.png)

Figure 2: block diagram in three columns headed On-peak Hour Input, Load Flexibility Measure and Results. The input is the on-peak hours in each state (summer, winter and intermediate peak start and end). The measure applies a relative set point offset during pre-peak and on-peak hours to the default set point schedule, with a random shift of -30 to 30 minutes, following a scenario design of pre-peak duration and offsets. Results are the baseline load profile and the profile after demand response.

Values for on-peak hours for summer months, winter months, and intermediate months are provided at the state level in an input file. The load flexibility measure first retrieves the heating and cooling set point schedules specific to each individual dwelling unit. It then modifies these schedules by adjusting the set points by an offset during the designated pre-peak and on-peak periods. This approach ensures that each unit's load flexibility aligns with its original comfort settings while providing targeted adjustments to reduce energy use during peak demand times. A minimum heating set point of 55°F and a maximum cooling set point of 82°F ensure that extreme discomfort is avoided. If the set point change would cause a heating set point higher than the original cooling set point or a cooling set point lower than the original heating set point, the set point adjustment is limited to avoid this condition. These thresholds and exceptions were chosen based on engineering judgment and only apply to a small percentage of dwelling units.

To prevent the creation of a new peak caused by the coincident return to normal set point temperatures, the load flexibility measure introduces a random shift to each dwelling unit's demand response start and stop time. The maximum allowable shift is defined in the scenario design, allowing each unit to randomly adjust its response start time within this range. For example, with a maximum random shift of 30 minutes and a 15-minute simulation time step, the potential random shift values are -30 minutes, -15 minutes, 0 minutes, 15 minutes, and 30 minutes.

## 3.3  Input Variables

There are two types of input variables: input variables for load flexibility scenario design and on-peak hour inputs. On-peak hour inputs are provided as a json file to indicate the peak hour start and end time at the state level. Table 5 presents a list of input variables and settings used for this analysis. These were based on the utility programs outlined in the technology overview in consultation with the demand flexibility modelers using the outputs of this analysis.

Table 5. Input Variables for HVAC Load Flexibility

| Variable Name                    | Description                                                                                                                                       | Value                                   |
|----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| loadflex_peak_offset             | Set point offset value during the peak period in degrees Fahrenheit. The set point is increased for cooling, and it is decreased for heating.     | 2 - 4°F                                 |
| loadflex_pre_peak_duration_hours | Duration of the pre-peak period in hours                                                                                                          | 1 - 4 hours                             |
| loadflex_pre_peak_offset         | Set point offset value during the pre-peak period in degrees Fahrenheit. The set point is decreased for cooling, and it is increased for heating. | 2 - 4°F                                 |
| loadflex_random_shift_minutes    | Maximum minutes to randomly shift the peak period. If the minutes are less than the time step, they will be assumed to be 0.                      | 30 minutes                              |
| peak_start_time                  | The time (local time) the peak period starts                                                                                                      | Varies by state and season; see Table 3 |

## 4 Results

## 4.1  Single-Building Examples

We performed an initial ResStock test run to validate the operation of the load flexibility measures. This was a test run performed before the final input values were established, which is why some values differ from the final selection. The test run was performed using 50 models spread across the nation with two scenarios (also called upgrades):

- Upgrade 1: load shifting plus load shedding -a pre-peak duration of 2 hours, a peak duration of 1 hour, and an offset of 2°F during both the pre-peak and on-peak period
- Upgrade 2: load shedding only -no pre-peak load shifting, a peak duration of 1 hour, and an offset of 2°F during the on-peak period.

Figure 3 shows the time-series thermostat set point for a dwelling unit in Delaware. Note that this dwelling unit has a temperature setback during the night. We can see that for upgrade 1, there is both a pre-peak and peak offset, with the peak period being 18:00 to 19:00. For upgrade 2, there is no pre-peak offset. Both show the expected temperature offset of 2°F.

Figure 3. Verification of set point changes

Three series, Upgrade 0, Upgrade 1 and Upgrade 2, are the heating set point. All follow the same daily schedule of a higher and a lower set point; once a day Upgrade 1 steps up above the others for a few hours and then drops below, and Upgrade 2 only drops. ## 1.2.5 Dispatch Strategy

In historic deployments, thermostat-based demand response is typically only dispatched 15 -25 days per year to avoid customer fatigue (Xcel, 2021) (Austin Energy, 2024). But the goal of this modeling is to create a dataset that can be analyzed to determine the maximum technical potential load profile impact at any given point in the year, so the demand flexibility is dispatched every day in the modeled dataset . The dispatch strategy is modified for shoulder-season days where heating or cooling load is assumed to be minimal, defined by an average daily temperature greater than 50°F and less than 68°F. On those days, load shifting (done via precooling or preheating) is not dispatched, but load-shedding events are dispatched. The method for choosing this temperature range is described in section 4.2 Initial Sensitivity Analysis. Because of the unrealistically high number of days that demand flexibility is dispatched in this upgrade, the results must be used thoughtfully. One approach is to use daily profiles from the baseline for most days of the year and to splice in daily profiles from the upgrade for days when the intent of the analysis is to dispatch demand flexibility. Similarly, annualized energy consumption or energy savings metrics should not be used because of the overrepresentation of dispatch .

## 2 ResStock Baseline Approach

The baseline assumption for thermostats in ResStock is a range of heating and cooling set points and setbacks or setups derived from the Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) 2020, which vary based on climate zone, building type, HVAC type, and tenure (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2023). These set points are assumed to apply year-round. Approximately one-third of dwelling units are assumed to have heating and/or cooling thermostat setbacks or setups, where the set point is changed by the homeowner during part of each day. The distribution of set points in the building stock is shown in Figure 1. ResStock makes no explicit assumption about whether these setbacks or setups are achieved using manual adjustment, a programmable thermostat, or a smart thermostat. In practice, demand response programs typically incentivize or directly pay for customers to install smart thermostats as a condition of program participation.

Figure 1. Distributions of thermostat set points, setups, and setbacks 1

## 3 Modeling Approach

## 3.1 Applicability

The goal of demand flexibility is to change the electric or gas load profile of the building in a meaningful way; therefore, this measure is applicable to all dwelling units with either a cooling system or a heating system. Although the measure shifts the load profile of the dwelling units with nonelectric heating during heating season, the change to the electric load profile is minimal because it only changes the fan or pump electricity consumption. For this reason, the heating load analysis in this document is focused on buildings with electric heating only. Table 4 summarizes the breakout of the building stock to which the measure applies and what is included in heating and cooling load analysis.

## 3.2  ResStock Workflow

Figure 2 illustrates the modeling approach used to integrate a load flexibility measure into ResStock. This measure modifies the existing building energy model thermostat set point schedules during the pre-peak and on-peak periods only. For times outside of the event, the existing thermostat schedules in the model are unchanged. If the baseline thermostat set point schedules indicate that the dwelling unit is already in a setback or a setup state, the demand flexibility thermostat change still applies.

The load flexibility scenario (which includes the pre-peak duration and the set point offset values) serves as input for the measure, allowing customized controls. The input values used for this measure are explained in section 3.3 Input Variables.

Figure 2. Modeling approach for running a load flexibility measure in ResStock

![Block diagram of the modeling approach: on-peak hour input, load flexibility measure, and results](93846_images/image_000003_06ad1ce32d34b0a4c47437dc4560d542e3896ac29aeb4ea0e7a85f2e95bb78c7.png)

Figure 2: block diagram in three columns headed On-peak Hour Input, Load Flexibility Measure and Results. The input is the on-peak hours in each state (summer, winter and intermediate peak start and end). The measure applies a relative set point offset during pre-peak and on-peak hours to the default set point schedule, with a random shift of -30 to 30 minutes, following a scenario design of pre-peak duration and offsets. Results are the baseline load profile and the profile after demand response.

Values for on-peak hours for summer months, winter months, and intermediate months are provided at the state level in an input file. The load flexibility measure first retrieves the heating and cooling set point schedules specific to each individual dwelling unit. It then modifies these schedules by adjusting the set points by an offset during the designated pre-peak and on-peak periods. This approach ensures that each unit's load flexibility aligns with its original comfort settings while providing targeted adjustments to reduce energy use during peak demand times. A minimum heating set point of 55°F and a maximum cooling set point of 82°F ensure that extreme discomfort is avoided. If the set point change would cause a heating set point higher than the original cooling set point or a cooling set point lower than the original heating set point, the set point adjustment is limited to avoid this condition. These thresholds and exceptions were chosen based on engineering judgment and only apply to a small percentage of dwelling units.

To prevent the creation of a new peak caused by the coincident return to normal set point temperatures, the load flexibility measure introduces a random shift to each dwelling unit's demand response start and stop time. The maximum allowable shift is defined in the scenario design, allowing each unit to randomly adjust its response start time within this range. For example, with a maximum random shift of 30 minutes and a 15-minute simulation time step, the potential random shift values are -30 minutes, -15 minutes, 0 minutes, 15 minutes, and 30 minutes.

## 3.3  Input Variables

There are two types of input variables: input variables for load flexibility scenario design and on-peak hour inputs. On-peak hour inputs are provided as a json file to indicate the peak hour start and end time at the state level. Table 5 presents a list of input variables and settings used for this analysis. These were based on the utility programs outlined in the technology overview in consultation with the demand flexibility modelers using the outputs of this analysis.

| loadflex_pre_peak_offset         | Set point offset value during the pre-peak period in degrees Fahrenheit. The set point is decreased for cooling, and it is increased for heating. | 2 - 4°F                                 |
| loadflex_random_shift_minutes    | Maximum minutes to randomly shift the peak period. If the minutes are less than the time step, they will be assumed to be 0.                      | 30 minutes                              |
| peak_start_time                  | The time (local time) the peak period starts                                                                                                      | Varies by state and season; see Table 3 |

## 4 Results

## 4.1  Single-Building Examples

We performed an initial ResStock test run to validate the operation of the load flexibility measures. This was a test run performed before the final input values were established, which is why some values differ from the final selection. The test run was performed using 50 models spread across the nation with two scenarios (also called upgrades):

- Upgrade 1: load shifting plus load shedding -a pre-peak duration of 2 hours, a peak duration of 1 hour, and an offset of 2°F during both the pre-peak and on-peak period
- Upgrade 2: load shedding only -no pre-peak load shifting, a peak duration of 1 hour, and an offset of 2°F during the on-peak period.

## Accessing Results

This documentation covers the ' HVAC Load Flexibility ' measure upgrade methodology and briefly discusses key results. All results can be accessed on the ResStock ™ Open Energy Data Initiative 'End -Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock' data lake and on the Data Viewer at resstock.nlr.gov.

## Measure Summary

| Measure Title | HVAC Load Flexibility |

| Measure Definition | This upgrade lowers the heating set point and increases the cooling set point during predefined on-peak hours. It can also preheat or precool the dwelling units for 1 to 4 hours, depending on the measure settings. |
| Applicability | This measure applies to all dwellings with either a heating system or a cooling system that is approximately 99.7% of the building stock. |
| Not Applicable | This measure does not apply to the dwelling units that have neither a heating system nor a cooling system - approximately 0.3% of the building stock. |
| Project Configuration File(s) | https://github.com/NatLabRockies/resstock/blob/sdr_2025_Release_1/project_national/sdr_upgrades_amy2018.yml |

## 1 Technology Summary

Renewable energy is increasingly being adopted for electricity generation. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that the share of U.S. power generation from renewables will increase from 21% in 2021 to 44% in 2050 (EIA, 2022). This projected increase consists mainly of new wind and solar power, but wind and solar power are inherently variable energy sources, which poses a challenge for grid stability and control compared to fossil fuel-based power generation. For instance, solar power generation fluctuates with the time of day and weather, whereas wind energy is influenced by seasonal and atmospheric conditions. These fluctuations require sophisticated grid management to ensure a stable electricity supply.

Flexible loads help balance supply and demand, especially as renewable energy increases. Many utility companies operate demand response programs. These programs range from interruptible service programs targeting large commercial and industrial customers, to rebates given to large customers for voluntary peak hour load reductions, to direct control of water heaters and air-conditioning compressors (Ryan Hledik A. R., 2022). Utilities such as Duke Energy (2024a), Xcel Energy (2024), and Pacific Gas and Electric Company (2024) enable demand response through time-based pricing where electricity rates vary by the time of day. By charging higher rates during peak hours and lower rates at other times, customers are encouraged to shift their usage to off-peak hours.

Residential buildings account for a substantial share of U.S. electricity demand, representing 38% of the total electricity consumption in 2023 (EIA, 2024), making this sector the largest of all sectors. Demand flexibility within the residential building stock is crucial to achieving demand-side load flexibility, which can help balance grid loads. Within the residential sector, most load flexibility potential is found within the heating and cooling end uses because of the inherent thermal energy storage capability of the building's heated or cooled mass.

This measure models the use of smart thermostats to achieve demand flexibility in residential buildings by controlling their heating and cooling systems. This document describes the technology in general, describes how it is modeled in ResStock ™ , and reviews results at a high level.

## 1.1  Introduction to Technology

According to Stewart (2023):

A smart thermostat is an internet-connected device that controls home heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) equipment and can automatically adjust temperature set points to optimize performance and achieve energy savings. Smart thermostat features often include two-way communication, occupancy detection (such as geofencing and occupancy sensors), schedule learning, and seasonal optimization algorithms. Smart thermostats can control most conventional HVAC systems including central air conditioners, heat pumps, and forced air furnaces.

Within the context of demand flexibility programs, the internet-connected feature of a smart thermostat is used by the utility (with customer consent) to remotely adjust the thermostat set points during target times. For example, Xcel Energy deploys Ecobee smart thermostats in their demand response program. These thermostats adjust customer home cooling set points by 1°F -4°F for up to 4 hours when there is a risk of an electricity shortage, as determined by Xcel Energy.

## 1.2  Technical Measure Details

Demand flexibility is commonly categorized into four groups: load shaping, load shifting, load shedding, and load shimmying (Peter Alstone, 2017). In this analysis, we consider load shifting and load shedding. In the following discussion, the peak period, or 'on -peak window,' is the window of time when the peak is to be reduced. The pre-peak window is the window of time immediately preceding the peak period.

## 1.2.1 Load Shifting

As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017) , load shifting ' represents DR [demand response] that encourages the movement of energy consumption from times of high demand to times when there is a surplus of renewable generation. Shift could smooth net load ramps associated with daily patterns of solar energy generation.'

For this analysis, load shifting is accomplished by preheating (for heating days) or precooling (for cooling days) the building prior to the on-peak window (during the pre-peak window). The idea is that the preheating or precooling increases the load prior to the on-peak window, conditions the indoor air, and preconditions the thermal mass and air in the building. Then the building requires less heating or cooling energy to maintain the set point during the on-peak window, reducing the overall load profile during this window. The extent of the load reduction will depend on the building 's characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, the infiltration, the duration of the preconditioning, and the timing of the peak period.

## 1.2.2  Load Shedding

As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017) , load shedding ' describes loads that can be curtailed to provide peak capacity and support the system in emergency or contingency events. '

For this analysis, load shedding is accomplished by decreasing the heating set point and increasing the cooling set point of the building during the on-peak window. This allows the temperature to drift beyond the original set point during the on-peak window, trading decreased thermal comfort for reduced peak load. How quickly the temperature drifts to the modified set point will depend on the building 's characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, and the infiltration.

## 1.2.3  Set Point Change and Magnitude

Different durations of pre-peak load shifting and different set point offsets for load shifting or load shedding can be applied by HVAC load flexibility programs. For a mild impact on residents, a shorter on-peak duration (e.g., 2 hours) with a small set point offset during the on-peak hour (e.g., 2°F) can be used. In contrast, for the maximum load change, a longer pre-peak period (e.g., 4 hours) with larger set point adjustments, such as a low precooling set point (e.g., 60°F) and/or a high on-peak cooling set point (e.g., 80°F), may be applied.

Table 1 outlines the pre-peak and on-peak durations as well as the set point offsets used in existing smart thermostat programs. Typically, on-peak periods last 1 -4 hours, and the set point is adjusted by 1 -4°F during peak periods to align with residents ' comfort preferences. Load-shifting preheating or precooling strategies are not widely adopted in the current programs surveyed for this analysis. These findings broadly match the findings reported in a 2024 market overview of demand flexibility programs (Sean Murphy, 2024).

Table 1. Load Flexibility Scenario Settings in Existing Smart Thermostat Programs

| Utility Company                         | Pre-Peak Duration   | On-Peak Duration   | Set Point Offset During Pre-Peak   | Set Point Offset During On-Peak   |
|-----------------------------------------|---------------------|--------------------|------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Pacific Gas and Electric Company (2024) | -                   | 1 - 4 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |
| Xcel (2021)                             | -                   | 1 - 6 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |
| Con Edison (2024)                       | -                   | 1 - 4 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |
| Duke Energy (2024b)                     | -                   | 1 - 4 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |
| Austin Energy (2024)                    | 1 - 30 minutes      | 2 hours            | 2°F                                | 1 - 4°F                           |
| National Grid (2024)                    | -                   | 1 - 4 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |

The appropriate pre-peak duration and set point offset depend on various factors, including a home ' s insulation quality, cooling system capacity, and weather conditions. Research suggests that pre-peak durations of 1 -4 hours and set point offsets of 2 to 6°F for preheating or precooling are effective strategies (German & Hoeschele, 2014). Table 2 presents the range of common settings for load flexibility based on existing smart thermostat programs and literature.

Table 2. Load Flexibility Dispatch Duration and Set Point Offset Summary

| Pre-Peak Duration   | Set Point Offset During Pre-Peak   | Set Point Offset During On- Peak   |
|---------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 1 - 4 hours         | 2 - 6°F                            | 1 - 4°F                            |

## 1.2.4 On-Peak Hour Identification

When analyzing the impact of load flexibility, it is necessary to define the target time periods when demand flexibility will be dispatched to reduce load. These time periods are commonly referred to as on-peak hours. On-peak hours can be identified in different ways, depending on the goal. For instance:

- Reducing system net load: Grid-wide net load data can be analyzed to identify hours with the highest demand, and demand flexibility can be dispatched to help lower overall system peak power generation requirements.
- Responding to time-of-use pricing: Utility rates for individual customers can be analyzed to identify times with the highest electricity prices. This is only applicable for customers with time-of-use rates. Demand flexibility can be dispatched to reduce individual customer utility bills.
- Minimizing grid operation costs: Grid-wide operational cost data can be analyzed to identify hours with the highest operational costs, which could be dependent on system

peak demand, renewable generation, and local or distribution-level peak power. Demand flexibility can be dispatched to help reduce overall system operation costs.

The primary use for the results from this analysis is to feed into a national-scale energy system analysis that extends to 2050. The hypothesis is that demand flexibility will play a more important role further in the future; therefore, for this measure, the goal is to quantify load flexibility's technical potential to reduce net system load in 2050. Cambium is a dataset of load profiles based on assumed changes to the power sector over time (Gagnon, et al., 2024). It provides future load projections and related metrics. The MidCase scenario within Cambium adopts central estimates for key inputs, including technology costs, fuel prices, and demand growth. One important note is that the Cambium data do not consider future changes in load profiles due to wide-scale electrification, such as the addition of electric vehicles or heat pumps. Future work intends to update these load profiles and reassess the peak period definitions.

This project uses 2050 net load data from Cambium's MidCase scenario (Gagnon, et al., 2024) to identify the peak hours for each state, categorized by summer months (June to September), winter months (January to March and December) and intermediate months (April to May and October to November). The definition of seasons as a uniform set of months across all states is imprecise, but given that the modeling is also based on forecasts of the power system in 2050, it was judged to be an acceptable simplification. The identified peak hour is applied consistently as the dispatch time for each day within the corresponding months for each state. On-peak period timing by state is shown in Table 3. The on-peak period is defined as the 4-hour window containing the peak load, not the exact hour of the peak load.

## 1 Technology Summary

Renewable energy is increasingly being adopted for electricity generation. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that the share of U.S. power generation from renewables will increase from 21% in 2021 to 44% in 2050 (EIA, 2022). This projected increase consists mainly of new wind and solar power, but wind and solar power are inherently variable energy sources, which poses a challenge for grid stability and control compared to fossil fuel-based power generation. For instance, solar power generation fluctuates with the time of day and weather, whereas wind energy is influenced by seasonal and atmospheric conditions. These fluctuations require sophisticated grid management to ensure a stable electricity supply.

Flexible loads help balance supply and demand, especially as renewable energy increases. Many utility companies operate demand response programs. These programs range from interruptible service programs targeting large commercial and industrial customers, to rebates given to large customers for voluntary peak hour load reductions, to direct control of water heaters and air-conditioning compressors (Ryan Hledik A. R., 2022). Utilities such as Duke Energy (2024a), Xcel Energy (2024), and Pacific Gas and Electric Company (2024) enable demand response through time-based pricing where electricity rates vary by the time of day. By charging higher rates during peak hours and lower rates at other times, customers are encouraged to shift their usage to off-peak hours.

Residential buildings account for a substantial share of U.S. electricity demand, representing 38% of the total electricity consumption in 2023 (EIA, 2024), making this sector the largest of all sectors. Demand flexibility within the residential building stock is crucial to achieving demand-side load flexibility, which can help balance grid loads. Within the residential sector, most load flexibility potential is found within the heating and cooling end uses because of the inherent thermal energy storage capability of the building's heated or cooled mass.

This measure models the use of smart thermostats to achieve demand flexibility in residential buildings by controlling their heating and cooling systems. This document describes the technology in general, describes how it is modeled in ResStock ™ , and reviews results at a high level.

## 1.1  Introduction to Technology

According to Stewart (2023):

A smart thermostat is an internet-connected device that controls home heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) equipment and can automatically adjust temperature set points to optimize performance and achieve energy savings. Smart thermostat features often include two-way communication, occupancy detection (such as geofencing and occupancy sensors), schedule learning, and seasonal optimization algorithms. Smart thermostats can control most conventional HVAC systems including central air conditioners, heat pumps, and forced air furnaces.

Within the context of demand flexibility programs, the internet-connected feature of a smart thermostat is used by the utility (with customer consent) to remotely adjust the thermostat set points during target times. For example, Xcel Energy deploys Ecobee smart thermostats in their demand response program. These thermostats adjust customer home cooling set points by 1°F -4°F for up to 4 hours when there is a risk of an electricity shortage, as determined by Xcel Energy.

## 1.2  Technical Measure Details

Demand flexibility is commonly categorized into four groups: load shaping, load shifting, load shedding, and load shimmying (Peter Alstone, 2017). In this analysis, we consider load shifting and load shedding. In the following discussion, the peak period, or 'on -peak window,' is the window of time when the peak is to be reduced. The pre-peak window is the window of time immediately preceding the peak period.

## 1.2.1 Load Shifting

As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017) , load shifting ' represents DR [demand response] that encourages the movement of energy consumption from times of high demand to times when there is a surplus of renewable generation. Shift could smooth net load ramps associated with daily patterns of solar energy generation.'

For this analysis, load shifting is accomplished by preheating (for heating days) or precooling (for cooling days) the building prior to the on-peak window (during the pre-peak window). The idea is that the preheating or precooling increases the load prior to the on-peak window, conditions the indoor air, and preconditions the thermal mass and air in the building. Then the building requires less heating or cooling energy to maintain the set point during the on-peak window, reducing the overall load profile during this window. The extent of the load reduction will depend on the building 's characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, the infiltration, the duration of the preconditioning, and the timing of the peak period.

## 1.2.2  Load Shedding

As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017) , load shedding ' describes loads that can be curtailed to provide peak capacity and support the system in emergency or contingency events. '

For this analysis, load shedding is accomplished by decreasing the heating set point and increasing the cooling set point of the building during the on-peak window. This allows the temperature to drift beyond the original set point during the on-peak window, trading decreased thermal comfort for reduced peak load. How quickly the temperature drifts to the modified set point will depend on the building 's characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, and the infiltration.

## 1.2.3  Set Point Change and Magnitude

Different durations of pre-peak load shifting and different set point offsets for load shifting or load shedding can be applied by HVAC load flexibility programs. For a mild impact on residents, a shorter on-peak duration (e.g., 2 hours) with a small set point offset during the on-peak hour (e.g., 2°F) can be used. In contrast, for the maximum load change, a longer pre-peak period (e.g., 4 hours) with larger set point adjustments, such as a low precooling set point (e.g., 60°F) and/or a high on-peak cooling set point (e.g., 80°F), may be applied.

Table 1 outlines the pre-peak and on-peak durations as well as the set point offsets used in existing smart thermostat programs. Typically, on-peak periods last 1 -4 hours, and the set point is adjusted by 1 -4°F during peak periods to align with residents ' comfort preferences. Load-shifting preheating or precooling strategies are not widely adopted in the current programs surveyed for this analysis. These findings broadly match the findings reported in a 2024 market overview of demand flexibility programs (Sean Murphy, 2024).

Table 1. Load Flexibility Scenario Settings in Existing Smart Thermostat Programs

| Xcel (2021)                             | -                   | 1 - 6 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |
| Con Edison (2024)                       | -                   | 1 - 4 hours        | -                                  | 1 - 4°F                           |

The appropriate pre-peak duration and set point offset depend on various factors, including a home ' s insulation quality, cooling system capacity, and weather conditions. Research suggests that pre-peak durations of 1 -4 hours and set point offsets of 2 to 6°F for preheating or precooling are effective strategies (German & Hoeschele, 2014). ## 1.2.4 On-Peak Hour Identification

When analyzing the impact of load flexibility, it is necessary to define the target time periods when demand flexibility will be dispatched to reduce load. These time periods are commonly referred to as on-peak hours. On-peak hours can be identified in different ways, depending on the goal. For instance:

- Reducing system net load: Grid-wide net load data can be analyzed to identify hours with the highest demand, and demand flexibility can be dispatched to help lower overall system peak power generation requirements.
- Responding to time-of-use pricing: Utility rates for individual customers can be analyzed to identify times with the highest electricity prices. This is only applicable for customers with time-of-use rates. Demand flexibility can be dispatched to reduce individual customer utility bills.
- Minimizing grid operation costs: Grid-wide operational cost data can be analyzed to identify hours with the highest operational costs, which could be dependent on system

peak demand, renewable generation, and local or distribution-level peak power. Demand flexibility can be dispatched to help reduce overall system operation costs.

The primary use for the results from this analysis is to feed into a national-scale energy system analysis that extends to 2050. The hypothesis is that demand flexibility will play a more important role further in the future; therefore, for this measure, the goal is to quantify load flexibility's technical potential to reduce net system load in 2050. Cambium is a dataset of load profiles based on assumed changes to the power sector over time (Gagnon, et al., 2024). It provides future load projections and related metrics. The MidCase scenario within Cambium adopts central estimates for key inputs, including technology costs, fuel prices, and demand growth. One important note is that the Cambium data do not consider future changes in load profiles due to wide-scale electrification, such as the addition of electric vehicles or heat pumps. Future work intends to update these load profiles and reassess the peak period definitions.

This project uses 2050 net load data from Cambium's MidCase scenario (Gagnon, et al., 2024) to identify the peak hours for each state, categorized by summer months (June to September), winter months (January to March and December) and intermediate months (April to May and October to November). The definition of seasons as a uniform set of months across all states is imprecise, but given that the modeling is also based on forecasts of the power system in 2050, it was judged to be an acceptable simplification. The identified peak hour is applied consistently as the dispatch time for each day within the corresponding months for each state. On-peak period timing by state is shown in Table 3. The on-peak period is defined as the 4-hour window containing the peak load, not the exact hour of the peak load.

## 4.3  Final Sensitivity Analysis

After further reviewing the real-world demand response programs and reviewing the initial sensitivity analysis results, we narrowed the analysis space. First, we narrowed the offset to only 2 -4°F, and then we limited the precooling windows to 1 hour and 4 hours. More details can be seen in Table 7.

In this round, we also introduced a random shift. This was used to reduce the 'snapback , ' or rebound, seen after the peak period when all thermostats reset to the normal set point at the same time. A maximum random shift of ± 30 minutes will make some buildings start their peak period up to 30 minutes early or up to 30 minutes late (i.e., the shift can be anything ranging from +30 minutes, to +15 minutes, to 0 minutes, to -15 minutes, to -30 minutes). This random shifting was assigned on a building-by-building basis, not on a per-event basis. In a real deployment, this staggering of individual homes could be accomplished through a combination of intentional control, inherent time delays, and equipment states found across the portfolio at any point in time.

## 4.5  Stock-Level Results

A test run with 30,000 samples was conducted. The state-level D3 metrics are calculated in the following five steps:

1. Filter out samples that have electric heating and samples that have cooling separately.

2. Aggregate state-level heating (or cooling) time series for both the baseline and savings from upgrades.
3. Calculate the percentage reduction in heating or cooling during the peak periods for each day.
4. Remove days where heating (or cooling) savings during peak periods are zero, indicating that the thermostat demand flexibility measure is not applicable on those days.
5. Compute the mean, along with the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles for the remaining days.

The results for the single-family detached across the five upgrades are shown in Figure 15 -Figure 19. States not shown in the figures either lack relevant data due to an insufficient sample size or do not have the specific end use (heating or cooling) savings.

Figure 15 shows an approximate 40% winter and 30% summer reduction in peak load from load shedding for 4 hours with a 2°F offset. As expected, Figure 16 shows an approximate 15% winter and 10% summer reduction from load shifting (preconditioning) for 4 hours with a 2°F offset. This lower reduction relative to Figure 15 is expected because the thermal inertia does not carry through the entire 4-hour peak window. Figure 17 shows an approximate 60% winter and 50% summer reduction in peak load from load shedding for 4 hours with a 4°F offset. This deep reduction is expected because of the significant depth of the set point change. Figure 18 shows an approximate 30% winter and 20% summer reduction from load shifting (preconditioning) for 4 hours with a 4°F offset. As expected, this reduction is larger than the reduction shown from load shifting with a 2°F offset because the deeper set point change for 4 hours allows more charging of the building thermal mass, allowing reduced space conditioning during more of the 4-hour peak window. Last, Figure 19 shows an approximate 10% winter and 5% summer reduction from load shifting (preconditioning) for 1 hour with a 2°F offset. This minimal impact is expected because the short duration of the preconditioning coupled with the small set point offset does not allow much charging of the building thermal mass, leading to a minimal impact during the peak window.

Figure 9. D3 percentage reduction of cooling energy consumption during the peak period for the whole year and at various pre-peak durations (including no pre-peak). The top figure shows a 2°F offset for both the pre-peak and peak periods, the middle shows a 4°F offset for both, and the bottom shows a 4°F offset for the peak period and a 6°F offset for the pre-peak period. Note that the ordering of the states varies.

<!-- figure described by overlay: resstock_resstock_amy2018_2025_release_1/upgrade_measures/measure_pdfs/93846.yaml

     method: vision-description

![Line chart of percent cooling reduction by state over the whole year, 4°F peak offset with 6°F pre-peak offset](93846_images/image_000012_129951035cfe5ecb59cd46b0a110748ac65b4708fa12fddfb92ed44233e3173b.png)

Figure 9, second bitmap: line chart titled 'Offset: Peak 4F, Pre-peak 6F', for the whole year. X-axis is state; y-axis is percent reduction, about 20 to 90. Six series are no pre-peak and pre-peak durations from 15 minutes to 4 hours. Reductions are about 65% to 88% in the leading state and about 23% to 27% in the last, with the lines crossing in a few low-reduction states.

Figure 10 shows an example of a heating day misclassified as a cooling day for a single model. The day was misclassified as a heating day, and preheating was performed from 14:00 to 18:00, resulting in a large reduction in cooling load later in the day because the preheating increased both the heating and the cooling set points 2 ; however, once the peak period begins at 18:00, the increased cooling set point is reset to normal, resulting in increased cooling energy consumption. Essentially, we tried to preheat when precooling would have been appropriate, resulting in increased load during the peak. The solution was to avoid preheating or precooling when the average daily outdoor temperature is near the threshold (66°F) because it is hard to predict whether precooling or preheating would be the more appropriate action. In the final run, we implemented this correction.

Figure 10. Anomalous demand response in a shoulder season day in Idaho

![Line chart of average cooling energy and outdoor temperature on a shoulder-season day in Idaho, with peak bands](93846_images/image_000013_23d53b26aa5e4186935f6d6eac63b188087cda48003e428010de7152ad96512d.png)

Figure 10: line chart from 09:00 on May 25 to 00:00 on May 26, 2020. Left axis is average cooling in kWh, 0 to about 0.45; right axis is temperature in °C for the outdoor temperature line. Shaded bands mark the pre-peak and peak periods, and the legend lists the baseline and the offset scenarios. Cooling is near zero until mid-afternoon, then spikes to roughly 0.25 to 0.3 kWh at the starts of the shaded periods.

To help decide the appropriate switchover temperatures, we looked at the distribution of the average heating and cooling loads during the peak period across various daily average temperatures, as shown in Figure 11 and Figure 12.

2 Preheating does not require raising the cooling set point by default -it only requires raising the heating set point; however, to prevent an inverted set point (where the cooling set point is lower than the heating set point), the algorithm raises the cooling set point as well when the heating set point exceeds the cooling set point.

Figure 11. State average hourly cooling load per building during the peak period

![Scatter plot of state average hourly cooling load during the peak period against daily average temperature](93846_images/image_000014_be750ad86d30b61c6abb090759d400be4aeb849dbc0794f50ea6eaa0fa2d29c9.png)

Figure 11: scatter plot, points coloured by state. X-axis is daily average temperature in °C, 0 to about 37; y-axis is cooling in kWh, 0 to 1.2. Cooling load is near zero below about 10°C and rises with temperature, reaching about 0.6 to 1.2 kWh at 30°C and above, with a wide spread between states at any one temperature.

Figure 12. State average hourly heating load per building during the peak period

![Scatter plot of state average hourly heating load during the peak period against daily average temperature](93846_images/image_000015_ef0017f010af5299bca91b9cb7119768ae4d1ffbb283ad5bb3fc89d27212a2fd.png)

Figure 12: scatter plot, points coloured by state. X-axis is daily average temperature in °C, -30 to 40; y-axis is average heating in kWh, 0 to 25. Heating load falls as temperature rises: the highest points, about 20 to 24 kWh, are at about -20°C, most points at 0°C are below about 12 kWh, and the load is near zero above about 20°C.

The average load at a given average daily temperature for a given state varies among different days (different dots in the figure), depending on the specific temperature profile for the day and the internal heat generated in the building via various occupancy-driven end uses. Figure 11 shows minimal cooling below an average daily temperature of 10°C (50°F), and Figure 12 shows minimal heating above an average daily temperature of 25°C (68°F). Based on these results, in the final implementation, we precooled only if the daily average temperature is above 68°F, and we preheated only if the daily average temperature is below 50°F.
